aAbout: God's Eye View is an open-source 3D world globe simulator — 'a spy-satellite simulator in your browser, except the data is real.' It renders Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles through Cesium and layers live aircraft, ships, satellites, earthquakes, traffic and public cameras from open sources, all processed locally in your browser. It went viral in 2026 for its voice-controlled AI agent, cockpit view and sensor-style visual modes. It is software you run yourself — via Pinokio one-click, a terminal install, or Docker — not a website you open.

aLink.label: WorldEye: the God's Eye View alternative

aStrengths: God's Eye View is the street-level, moving world: live aircraft, ships, satellites, earthquakes and public cameras on a photorealistic 3D globe, plus cockpit view, sensor looks (FLIR, night vision) and a voice agent that flies and tracks on command — all free, all running on your machine with source you can inspect and extend. Where Worldview looks down at the planet's systems from orbit, God's Eye View puts you inside the scene those systems are moving through. For creators, tinkerers and live watchers, nothing scientific matches its immediacy.
bAbout: NASA Worldview is NASA EOSDIS's free, open-source browser for near-real-time satellite imagery: more than 1,000 global, full-resolution layers — fires, storms, air quality, sea ice, vegetation and more — most updated within about three hours of observation, some spanning nearly 30 years. It adds event pins for cyclones, wildfires and eruptions, time-lapse animation building, layer comparison (swipe and opacity) and downloadable underlying data via NASA's GIBS services. No signup; it runs in the browser.
bStrengths: NASA Worldview is an extraordinary free research tool: 1,000+ full-resolution satellite layers, most refreshed within ~3 hours, geostationary imagery in 10-minute increments, event tracking for cyclones, wildfires and eruptions, custom time-lapse animations and comparison tools — open source, backed by NASA's EOSDIS, with the data itself downloadable. For environmental science and disaster analysis, its scientific layer library is unmatched at any price, let alone free.
betterAnswer: They answer different questions. God's Eye View is a free, open-source 3D globe you run on your own computer — built for live movement: aircraft, ships, satellites and cameras in a photoreal scene you can talk to. NASA Worldview is NASA's hosted instrument — built for processes: 1,000+ scientific satellite layers, hours old, with time-lapse and downloadable data. If you want to watch the planet move, install God's Eye View; if you want to study how its systems are changing, open NASA Worldview.
consA: You must install and run it yourself (Pinokio, terminal or Docker)
Camera layer is small (~4,000) beside hosted atlases
Ships need a free third-party key; voice spends your OpenAI credit
No science-layer library or downloadable research data
No general history archive — only specific timelines such as weather and launches
consB: No live cameras, aircraft or vessel tracking at all
A working research console — not a casual, cinematic explorer
No photorealistic 3D globe or street-level view
Event pins highlight active events, but there are no push alerts

faqs.a: No — they are unrelated products. God's Eye View is free open-source software by Bilawal Sidhu and Sameh Khamis that you install and run locally. NASA Worldview is NASA EOSDIS's hosted browser for satellite imagery. They share open data and little else.
faqs.q: Is God's Eye View the same as NASA Worldview?

faqs.a: Yes. The software is free and open source under the MIT licence. The only costs are optional third-party ones you control: the voice agent uses your own OpenAI API credit (the app warns at $2 and caps at $5 per session), and photoreal 3D tiles can be metered if you use a direct Google key instead of the free Cesium ion route.
faqs.q: Is God's Eye View really free?

faqs.a: More than 1,000 global layers — satellite imagery and science products covering fires, storms, air quality, temperature, sea ice, vegetation and hundreds of other variables, many updated near-real-time.
faqs.q: How many layers does NASA Worldview have?

faqs.a: Only God's Eye View: its CCTV Mesh layer states a shared cap of about 4,000 cameras, projected into its 3D scene. NASA Worldview has no camera network — it shows the planet from orbit. For comparison, WorldEye's directory lists 74,229 public cameras.
faqs.q: Which has live cameras, God's Eye View or NASA Worldview?

faqs.a: No. NASA Worldview runs in the browser with no signup. God's Eye View is the opposite: no account at all, but you install it on your own computer first.
faqs.q: Do I need to install anything for NASA Worldview?

faqs.a: NASA Worldview: most of its layers update within about three hours of satellite observation, with geostationary imagery in 10-minute increments. God's Eye View's live feeds refresh far faster — its own notes put most feeds at every 15–30 seconds — but they are movement data (flights, ships, cameras), not full-resolution science imagery.

intro: God's Eye View and NASA Worldview both promise the real planet, free — from opposite altitudes. God's Eye View is open-source software (by Bilawal Sidhu and Sameh Khamis) that you install on your own computer: a photorealistic 3D globe alive with flights, ships, satellites and cameras, driven by voice. NASA Worldview is NASA's hosted instrument: over a thousand scientific satellite layers refreshed within hours, built for watching fires, storms, ice and oceans change. One puts you inside the moving world; the other looks down on its systems.
pricingA: There is no God's Eye View price or subscription — the software is free and open source. The README's own cost table is honest about the edges: most layers cost $0 with no signup; a free-key tier (AISStream, NASA FIRMS, Cesium ion within quota) unlocks more; the voice agent spends your own OpenAI credit with a $2 warning and $5 hard cap per session; and photoreal tiles through a direct Google key are metered by Google.
pricingB: Completely free — NASA provides Worldview as a public service through EOSDIS. No paid plans, and no signup is required to browse.
prosA: Completely free and open source (MIT) — no subscription, ever
Live flights, ships, satellites, earthquakes and cameras on one 3D globe
Voice-controlled AI agent — talk to the globe
Runs locally: your data and keys stay on your machine
Endlessly extendable — every layer is a module
prosB: 1,000+ full-resolution satellite layers, most hours old
Event pins for cyclones, wildfires and eruptions
Time-lapse animations, layer comparison and downloadable data
Completely free from NASA — no signup, open source

verdictA: Choose God's Eye View if you want the planet in motion at ground level — live flights, ships, cameras and satellites on a photoreal 3D globe you control by voice — and you're comfortable installing software to get it free and open forever.
verdictB: Choose NASA Worldview if you watch systems — tracking a wildfire's spread, a hurricane's approach, sea-ice retreat or air-quality plumes with imagery that is hours old, across 1,000+ layers, free from NASA.
verdictLine: God's Eye View is the view from inside the scene — live movement on a photoreal 3D globe you own. NASA Worldview is the view from orbit — the deepest free record of the planet's changing systems. The first is software you install; the second is an instrument you simply open.
worldEye: If installing software is the dealbreaker in God's Eye View, and NASA Worldview's science console has no cameras or live movement, WorldEye is the middle path: a hosted 3D globe that opens free in any browser with no signup at all — 74,229 public cameras across 105 countries, live flights, ships, satellites, weather, earthquakes and wildfires in the same view. Its imagery is neither NASA's 1,000-layer science library nor God's Eye View's photoreal 3D tiles, and it doesn't claim to be; its Pro tier ($7.99/week, $13.99/month or $74.99/year) buys an OSINT toolkit and intel feeds rather than research data.
